title: Devil with a Blue Dress On

meta.title: Who originally recorded "Devil with a Blue Dress On"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Mitch Ryder original. Shorty Long wrote it with Mickey Stevenson and cut it first in March 1964 — the debut single on Motown’s Soul label.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Devil with a Blue Dress On'?
meta.ogDescription: Everyone credits Mitch Ryder’s 1966 medley. Shorty Long recorded it first, in March 1964, on Motown’s Soul label, and far slower.

answer.label: Not a Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels original — a 1964 Shorty Long single on Motown
answer.originalArtistDates: 1940–1969 · American soul singer, songwriter and Motown multi-instrumentalist
answer.sourceLine: Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels’ frantic 1966 medley with ‘Good Golly, Miss Molly’ hit No. 4 and is so completely identified with the band that the song is generally taken to be theirs. It is not. ‘Devil with a Blue Dress On’ was written by Shorty Long with Motown A&R chief William ‘Mickey’ Stevenson, and Long recorded it first — issued in March 1964 as Soul 35001, the very first record released on Motown’s new Soul imprint. Long’s original is a slower, bluesier stomp, and it went nowhere: it missed the Hot 100 entirely and sat at No. 125 on the ‘Bubbling Under’ chart. The speed is Ryder’s invention; the song is Long’s.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Motown
original.released: Issued in March 1964 as a 7-inch 45 on Soul 35001 — the first record ever released on Motown’s new Soul imprint, a subsidiary set up for its more blues-leaning artists. It was Shorty Long’s debut single for the label, backed with ‘Wind It Up’, and the A-side ran 2:49. The label read simply ‘Devil With The Blue Dress’ — the ‘On’ that every later discography attaches was not on the original release.
original.charted: Barely at all. It missed the Billboard Hot 100 and stalled at No. 125 on the ‘Bubbling Under’ chart. A figure of No. 26 R&B is widely repeated, but it should be treated with care: Billboard had suspended its R&B singles chart from 30 November 1963 until 23 January 1965, so there was no Billboard R&B chart in existence in March 1964 — and Wikipedia’s own article on Shorty Long says the single never charted nationally.
original.cover: Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels, September 1966 on New Voice — produced by Bob Crewe and cut at Bell Sound Studios in New York as a 3:01 medley with Little Richard’s ‘Good Golly, Miss Molly’, backed with ‘I Had It Made’. It reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100, the band’s highest-charting single, and Rolling Stone later placed it at No. 428 on its 500 Greatest Songs list.

trail: The song was written by Shorty Long and William ‘Mickey’ Stevenson and, in Wikipedia’s words, was ‘first recorded by Long in 1964’; the same page dates Mitch Ryder’s version to September 1966 on New Voice Wikipedia ↗.

The Motown singles chronicle Motown Junkies logs the release as ‘Soul S 35001 (A), March 1964’, backed with ‘Wind It Up’ — and notes that most discographies add an ‘On’ the original label never carried Motown Junkies ↗.
The discographic record agrees: MusicBrainz has the 1964 US 7-inch on Soul, catalogue 35001, with Shorty Long’s 2:49 A-side and ‘Wind It Up’ on the flip MusicBrainz ↗.
Wikidata is unambiguous about which record is the source: entity Q5267354 is described as ‘1964 single by Shorty Long’, with Ryder’s recording listed beneath it as a later performance Wikidata ↗.

authors.name: Shorty Long
authors.heading: About Shorty Long
authors.metaLine: 1940–1969 · American soul singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist
authors.bio: Frederick Earl ‘Shorty’ Long (born 20 May 1940 in Birmingham, Alabama) came to Motown in 1963 and was handed a distinction almost nobody else got: besides Smokey Robinson, he was the only Motown artist of the 1960s allowed to produce his own recordings. He sang and played piano, organ, drums, harmonica and trumpet, and served as MC for the Motortown Revue tours. ‘Devil With The Blue Dress’ was his debut single and the first record on Motown’s Soul imprint; his one big hit came later, with ‘Here Comes the Judge’ in 1968. He drowned on 29 June 1969, aged 29, when a boat crashed on the Detroit River — Stevie Wonder played harmonica at his burial.

authors.name: Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on Mitch Ryder
authors.metaLine: American rock band · Detroit · formed out of Billy Lee & the Rivieras
authors.bio: Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels were a Detroit band renamed after they met producer Bob Crewe, who cast Ryder as a blue-eyed soul shouter fronting a horn-driven group. Their run on New Voice — ‘Jenny Take a Ride!’ at No. 10, the ‘Devil with a Blue Dress On / Good Golly, Miss Molly’ medley at No. 4, ‘Sock It to Me – Baby!’ at No. 6 — is one of the great sustained bursts of mid-sixties American rock and roll. The medley is genuinely, thrillingly theirs: the breakneck tempo, the segue into Little Richard, the sheer noise of it. The only thing that is not theirs is the song.

authors.name: William ‘Mickey’ Stevenson
authors.heading: About Mickey Stevenson
authors.metaLine: b. 4 January 1937 · Detroit · Motown’s head of A&R
authors.bio: William ‘Mickey’ Stevenson co-wrote the song with Shorty Long. Born in Detroit on 4 January 1937, he ran Motown’s A&R department through the label’s peak years and organised the in-house studio band that became known as the Funk Brothers — arguably his largest single contribution to twentieth-century pop. His writing credits include ‘Dancing in the Street’, ‘Pride and Joy’ and ‘It Takes Two’. That a man with that resume is invisible on a song most people file under ‘Mitch Ryder’ is a fair summary of how songwriting credit travels.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nothing about the Mitch Ryder record is fake or wrong — it is simply a cover, and a spectacular one. The error is purely chronological: a 1966 hit taken for the point of origin, when the song had already been written, recorded and released on Motown by a man almost nobody remembers.

items.why: Ryder’s version was released in September 1966 on New Voice. The song was written by Shorty Long and Mickey Stevenson and first recorded by Long in 1964 the history ↗.
Long’s single was the first record issued on Motown’s Soul imprint, backed with ‘Wind It Up’ and running 2:49 — a slower, bluesier reading of the same song the release ↗.

items.tag: neither is in the famous band
items.why: Long wrote it and cut it; Stevenson, Motown’s head of A&R, co-wrote it. Both credits survive intact on the Ryder record — they are simply never read Stevenson ↗.
The 1964 Soul label carried the title without the trailing ‘On’. The longer form most people know came with the cover and was retro-fitted to the original by later discographies.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Shorty Long with Mickey Stevenson, first recorded by Long and released in March 1964 on Soul 35001, and made famous — but not originated — by Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels in 1966 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: A cover normally has to displace something to take over. This one did not: there was nothing in the way. Shorty Long’s original never reached the Billboard Hot 100 at all — it stopped at No. 125 on the ‘Bubbling Under’ chart — so by the time Mitch Ryder’s version arrived in 1966, the American listening public had, for practical purposes, never heard the song. Ryder’s record did not overwrite a memory; it created one.

What Ryder and producer Bob Crewe changed was tempo and context. Long’s 1964 record is a mid-paced, blues-rooted Motown stomp. Ryder’s is a sprint, welded to a rearrangement of Little Richard’s ‘Good Golly, Miss Molly’ and cut at Bell Sound in New York into a single 3:01 rush. The medley form is the tell: nobody builds a medley out of a song they consider untouchable, and nobody hearing that version first would guess the source record was the slower one. Bruce Springsteen then spent decades playing it as part of his live ‘Detroit Medley’, which bolted the song even harder to Ryder’s city and Ryder’s tempo.
detailsBody: Shorty Long writes the song at Motown with the label’s head of A&R, William ‘Mickey’ Stevenson.
Long records it and Motown issues it in March 1964 as Soul 35001 — the first release on the brand-new Soul imprint — backed with ‘Wind It Up’ and titled simply ‘Devil With The Blue Dress’.
The original misses the Hot 100, reaching only No. 125 on ‘Bubbling Under’.
Mitch Ryder & the Detroit Wheels record it at Bell Sound Studios in New York with Bob Crewe producing, as a far faster medley with ‘Good Golly, Miss Molly’.
New Voice releases the medley in September 1966; it reaches No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and becomes the band’s biggest hit.
Bruce Springsteen adopts it into his live ‘Detroit Medley’ from the 1970s onward, and it appears on the 1980 No Nukes concert album — in Ryder’s arrangement, at Ryder’s tempo.
context.pull: The tempo is Mitch Ryder’s. The song is Shorty Long’s.
